concepts.topicTitle: Concept of Markets and the Law of Demand
concepts.label: Demand and the Law of Demand
concepts.cardText: Prices do not change randomly; they react to what people want, how much is available, the seasons, festivals, trends and sometimes rumours. The prices of all goods and services are determined by two forces, demand and supply. Demand is the quantity of a product that people are willing and able to buy at a particular price, depending on their needs, preferences, season, trend and income; it is not just the desire to buy but willingness complemented by the ability or purchasing power to buy. When the price of a product rises, the quantity demanded decreases, and when it falls, the quantity demanded increases: this is the Law of Demand, the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded. Individual demand is the quantity one consumer wants at different prices, keeping other factors constant, shown as a demand schedule and plotted as a downward-sloping demand curve. Market demand is the sum of all individual demand.

concepts.topicTitle: Concept of Markets and the Law of Demand
concepts.label: Other Determinants of Demand
concepts.cardText: Demand does not change only because of price: many other factors influence how much people want to buy even when the price stays the same. The price of related goods matters: substitute goods can replace each other, like tea and coffee, so if the price of one rises demand for the other increases; complementary goods are used together, like smartphones and earphones, so if the demand for printers rises the demand for cartridges may rise too. Rising household income lets consumers buy more or higher-quality products. Taste and preference decide demand, and population size and composition matter. Diminishing marginal utility means the additional usefulness from a product declines as more is consumed, so willingness to pay and demand fall. Seasonality changes demand with weather, festivals and cultural habits. Future price expectations matter: expecting prices to fall, consumers postpone purchases; expecting them to rise, they buy immediately.

concepts.topicTitle: Producer Behaviour and the Law of Supply
concepts.label: Supply and the Law of Supply
concepts.cardText: Supply is the quantity of a product that sellers are willing and able to offer at a particular price. As price increases, quantity supplied increases, and as price decreases, quantity supplied falls, because higher prices increase profitability, incentivising producers to increase output and attracting new firms to the market. This is the law of supply. Individual supply is the quantity a particular seller offers at different prices; at Rs 50 a seller supplies 1 kg of mangoes, at Rs 100 2 kg and at Rs 150 3 kg, giving an upward-sloping supply curve. Market supply is the sum of all individual supplies, obtained by adding the quantities of all sellers at each price. At the start of the mango season supply is low, making mangoes costly; mid-season supply increases and prices fall. When supply is less than demand prices rise; when supply exceeds demand prices fall.

concepts.topicTitle: Producer Behaviour and the Law of Supply
concepts.label: Other Determinants of Supply
concepts.cardText: Besides price, several factors change supply. The price of related goods: if wheat prices are low but chickpea prices are high, a farmer will grow more chickpeas, so the supply of one good depends on the profitability of other alternatives for the supplier. The number of sellers: more sellers mean greater competition and increased production, so supply exceeds demand and prices fall; fewer sellers mean lower supply than demand and rising prices. Technology: improvement reduces the cost of production, allowing producers to produce and supply more, as with drip irrigation and weather sensors, or cold storage that carries mangoes to distant markets. Future expectations: if producers expect a boom in demand they produce more, and if they expect lower demand they cut production; potato wholesalers expecting prices to rise may hold back supply now to sell later.

concepts.topicTitle: Market Equilibrium, Price Determination and Government Intervention
concepts.label: Market Equilibrium and Price Determination
concepts.cardText: Every market involves negotiation between what buyers are willing to pay and what sellers are willing to accept, so prices are determined by the interaction between demand and supply. At a lower price there is excess demand, whereas at a higher price there is excess supply. Market equilibrium is the point where the supply of goods and services equals demand, so there is no excess supply (surplus) or excess demand (shortage) and prices tend to remain stable unless external factors change. In the mango example at Rs 100 the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied at 12 kg: the equilibrium price is Rs 100 and the equilibrium quantity 12 kg. At this point there is no pressure for prices to change and the market is 'cleared'. On a graph, equilibrium is where the demand curve intersects the supply curve.

concepts.topicTitle: Market Equilibrium, Price Determination and Government Intervention
concepts.label: Does Market Equilibrium Exist in the Real World?
concepts.cardText: In theory equilibrium is an intersection point between demand and supply, but in the real world markets are dynamic, with constantly changing conditions: technology, wages, interest rates, wars, political events, pandemics, weather and natural disasters alter demand and supply. So equilibrium in the real world is never stable and moves all the time; the market is always adjusting to a new equilibrium, never fully settling at the previous one. During the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 demand for face masks surged and supply could not catch up immediately, so the price rose significantly; over time suppliers adjusted and prices fell, and after the pandemic demand reduced and prices returned to pre-pandemic levels. Hotel tariffs show dynamic markets: a Goa hotel's room price changes with season, weekends and New Year's Eve, and may be cut overnight to fill empty rooms.

concepts.topicTitle: Market Equilibrium, Price Determination and Government Intervention
concepts.label: The Role of Government in the Market
concepts.cardText: India is the fourth-largest economy in the world, a market-based, regulated economy in which prices depend on demand and supply. But markets do not always work fairly: they allocate goods and services based on willingness and ability to pay, so essential goods like medicines could become inaccessible. Fairness and equity in allocation are needed, particularly for vulnerable and low-income groups. The government regulates unfair practices to protect consumers, workers and producers: a price ceiling sets the maximum a seller can charge, as for essential medicines; a minimum wage is a price floor. A monopoly, a single or few sellers dominating a market, can charge higher prices, supply less and provide poorer quality, so the government keeps prices and quantity in check. Regulators like RBI, the Central Consumer Protection Authority, TRAI and SEBI ensure transparency. During COVID-19 the government declared sanitisers essential commodities under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955, capping the retail price. The government also provides public goods such as roads, parks, streetlights and defence, which private firms do not supply because they give no direct profit and people may free-ride.

concepts.topicTitle: Market Equilibrium, Price Determination and Government Intervention
concepts.label: Limitations of Government Intervention
concepts.cardText: Although government regulations are required when markets are inefficient, they must be implemented carefully, because excessive intervention can have adverse effects. Price distortions and reduced producer incentives: if the government fixes prices below market levels, such as a maximum wheat price of Rs 20 per kg when the market sets Rs 30, farmers receive less than in a free market, which may reduce production and cause shortages. Compliance burdens: extensive regulations, licences, permits and procedures hurt businesses, especially small enterprises, and hamper ease of doing business; a small restaurant may need many permissions on food safety, fire safety and pollution control. Discouraging innovation and entrepreneurship: heavy regulation and price controls reduce incentives to invest in new ideas or technology, reducing long-term productivity. Markets are dynamic systems that constantly adapt, and the government intervenes when markets fail, under-provide public goods or enable monopolies, but excessive regulation can also harm.
